sceneHappening: Do not be shaken: the day of the Lord has not come, and a rebellion and the lawless one come first
summary: Concerning the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ and their gathering together to him, Paul asks them "not to be quickly shaken in your mind, or troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by letter as from us, saying that the day of the Lord has come." Let no one deceive them in any way, for that day will not come "unless the departure comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of destruction, he who opposes and exalts himself against all that is called God or that is worshiped; so that he sits as God in the temple of God, setting himself up as God." Don't they remember that when Paul was still with them, he told them these things? Now they know what restrains him, so that in his own time he may be revealed. "For the mystery of lawlessness already works. Only there is one who restrains now, until he is taken out of the way. Then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth, and bring to nothing by the brightness of his coming; even he whose coming is according to the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all deception of wickedness for those who are perishing, because they didn't receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved. Because of this, God sends them a working of error, that they should believe a lie; that they all might be judged who didn't believe the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness." But Paul and his friends are bound to give thanks to God always for them, brothers loved by the Lord, because God chose them from the beginning for salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief in the truth, to which he called them through the gospel, "for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." So then, brothers, "stand firm, and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word, or by letter from us." Now may the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, "comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word."
whySettingMatters: This chapter is among the most debated in the New Testament, and Paul himself says he had already told them details that we do not have (2:5-6). The immediate concern is plain: someone, by a prophecy, a spoken report, or a letter claiming to be from Paul, said that the day of the Lord had already come, and the Thessalonians were alarmed. Paul says it has not, and that certain things must happen first: a "rebellion" (the Greek word apostasia usually means a revolt or falling away) and the revealing of "the man of lawlessness." Who or what that figure is has been argued over from the early church to today: suggestions include a Roman emperor (Caligula had tried to put his statue in the Jerusalem temple in AD 40; Nero was later a candidate), a future individual often called the Antichrist, a religious or political system, or a symbol of rebellion against God in every age. "The temple of God" might be the Jerusalem temple or the church. "What restrains" him is also debated: it has been read as the Roman Empire and its law, the preaching of the gospel, the Holy Spirit, or an angel, and Paul does not name it. What can be said is that Paul's purpose is pastoral: do not be shaken; the Lord will destroy lawlessness by the breath of his mouth, and God has chosen them for salvation. The mention of letters "as from us" shows that forged letters were a real concern in the early church.

people.note: Corrects a rumor and asks them not to be shaken.
Alarmed by a report that the day had come; chosen for salvation.
The rebel and "son of destruction" who comes before the day.
Whose working is behind the lawless one.
Who will bring the lawless one to nothing by the breath of his mouth.

questions: Paul's first aim is to stop the Thessalonians being "shaken" and "alarmed." What does that say about how he wants to use teaching on the end?
Paul says he told them things we do not have. What can we do when a passage depends on shared knowledge we no longer have?
The "man of lawlessness" has been identified in many ways. What does the number of answers suggest about how humbly to hold them?
The chapter ends with thanks and a prayer for comfort and strength. How does that frame the difficult middle?
